traveler: María Estela Martínez Cartas de Perón (Isabel Perón)
title: The Dancer, the Delegate, the President: from a La Rioja birth certificate to a Madrid house with no grave in it
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: La Rioja, the birth certificate
stops.date_confidence: attested; both the Spanish and English biographical records give 4 February 1931
stops.campa: In the provincial capital of La Rioja, under the dry foothills, María Estela Martínez Cartas is born on the fourth of February 1931, one of several children of a bank employee. The name Isabel is not yet hers; she will take it later, off a stage. Nothing in the household marks the child for anything. There is no politics in it and no line into the Buenos Aires that decides Argentina. Forty-three years on she will sign decrees as the first woman anywhere to hold the title of President of a republic. La Rioja keeps the certificate and, for now, nothing else.
suggested_refs: The civil birth register of the city of La Rioja, 4 February 1931

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Cresto house
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year of the move is given without a month or day, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Her father dies and the family goes down to Buenos Aires. The girl is raised largely in the household of José Cresto and Isabel Zoila Gómez de Cresto, treated as adoptive parents without papers to say so, and from that woman she takes, by one account, the name she will carry the rest of her life. There are piano lessons and a Catholic schooling that stops early. The family has little money and some respectability. The city she enters at seven is the city she will govern and be flown out of under arrest.
suggested_refs: The Cresto household in Buenos Aires, informal guardians of the child María Estela

stops.name: Teatro Nacional Cervantes, the corps de ballet
stops.date_confidence: disputed; one summary gives 1950, the Spanish record says she entered at twenty, which places it c. 1951 given a February 1931 birth. The atlas does not resolve it
stops.campa: At twenty she enters the corps de ballet attached to the Teatro Nacional Cervantes, the state house on Libertad with its imported Valencian tilework and its permanent shortage of money. The training is Spanish dance above all, the repertoire what a touring company can carry into a provincial hall. She is a working dancer, not a star, in a profession that in Argentina in 1951 sits one step above the cabaret. The state that pays her by the season will be hers to run in twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Nacional Cervantes, Libertad 815, San Nicolás, and its ballet company payrolls of the early 1950s

stops.name: Córdoba, the interior circuit
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the touring years are given as a span, 1952 to 1954, and pinned here to the opening year
stops.campa: With a traveling company she works the interior: Córdoba, Entre Ríos, Santa Fe, the halls and cinemas of provincial capitals, and across the river to Montevideo for Uruguayan engagements. This is the Argentina the delegate of 1965 will tour again by air, with crowds waiting at every airstrip, seen first from the wrong side of the footlights and paid by the night. Juan Perón is president of the country she is crossing. Eva Perón dies in Buenos Aires in July 1952 while the company is on the road, and the nation stops for ten days.
suggested_refs: Provincial theatre programmes of Córdoba, Entre Ríos and Santa Fe, 1952-1954

stops.name: Teatro Avenida, the name Isabel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1953; no month given, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Back in the capital she joins the dance company of the Teatro Avenida on Avenida de Mayo and shares the stage with Haydée Padilla. Here the stage name is fixed: Isabel, one word, on the program. The Avenida is a Spanish house, zarzuela and flamenco, six blocks from the Casa Rosada along the same avenue the crowds walk on the days that matter. She is twenty-two. In the Casa Rosada at the far end of those six blocks, Juan Perón has two years left of his government.
suggested_refs: The 1953 season of the Teatro Avenida dance company, Av. de Mayo 1222

segments.name: The Tour That Ends in Panama

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the tour leaves the country
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955; the tour's internal dates are not itemized, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: A South American ballet tour with Faustino García's company takes her out of Argentina: Santiago de Chile first, then Lima and Bogotá, an itinerary of cheap hotels and one-week bookings. In September 1955 the Revolución Libertadora throws Juan Perón out of the Casa Rosada and onto a Paraguayan gunboat in the river; the dancer reads it in foreign newspapers in a country not her own. Two exiles are now moving north up the same continent by different means, and neither knows the other exists.
suggested_refs: The 1955 South American tour of the Faustino García ballet company

stops.name: Panama City, the last engagement of the road
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1955; the day is not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The tour reaches Panama in December and books into the cabaret circuit of the isthmus, the last engagement of a two-year road. The city is full of transients: canal traffic, American servicemen, and a small colony of Latin American politicians in flight from their own armies. Sources differ on the venue of the meeting that follows and on whether it happens in this city or up the line at Colón; they agree it happens in Panama within weeks of her arrival. She is twenty-four and has a contract to finish.
suggested_refs: The Panama City cabaret and theatre circuit of 1955-1956, venue of the first Perón meeting

stops.name: Colón, the exile buys out her contract
stops.date_confidence: disputed; the Spanish record puts the meeting in December 1955 or January 1956, a Britannica-derived summary gives 1960. Both place it in Panama. The atlas keeps the corpus pin and the earlier date and flags the conflict
stops.campa: The exiled Juan Perón, fifty-nine, four months out of the Casa Rosada, keeps rooms on the isthmus and comes to see the Argentine dancer perform. He buys out her contract. Within weeks she is living with him, thirty-five years his junior, and the ballet ends. The atlas already holds this pin from his side: the widower of Eva Perón, who has lost track of his wife's embalmed body somewhere in Europe, taking up with a woman young enough to be his daughter in a country neither of them may stay in.
suggested_refs: juan_peron.journey.json, stop 'Colón, Panama: the exile and the meeting with Isabel'

stops.name: Caracas, the rented rooms and the embassy
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1956; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: They move to Caracas in August and live modestly on Perón's shrinking money, watched by Venezuelan police and by Argentine agents who report home. She keeps the house and types his letters. The exile household has a trade of its own and she learns it: who visits, who is a spy, which government will tolerate them next. In January 1958 the fall of Pérez Jiménez turns the city over to the street and the couple takes refuge inside the Dominican Republic's embassy before flying out. The exact building is not named in the sources consulted.
suggested_refs: The Dominican Republic embassy in Caracas, refuge of the Perón household in January 1958

stops.name: Ciudad Trujillo, two years under the Benefactor
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1958; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Rafael Trujillo receives them in Ciudad Trujillo and they stay nearly two years under the protection of the hemisphere's most durable dictator. Perón receives Argentine delegations and runs by mail a movement outlawed at home; Isabel is the one who sorts that mail and cooks for the visitors. This is the third country in two years. There is no evidence she asked for any of it, and none that she resisted it; the record shows her present at every address, doing the household work of a government in exile.
suggested_refs: The Perón residence in Ciudad Trujillo, 1958-1960, under Rafael Trujillo's protection

stops.name: Madrid, the villa 17 de Octubre at Puerta de Hierro
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 26 January 1960
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of January 1960 the household reaches Madrid and settles at Puerta de Hierro, in the villa Perón names 17 de Octubre, under Franco's tolerance and Franco's surveillance. The corpus already carries this pin twice: eighteen years of Juan Perón's exile, and later the coffin of Eva Perón. Isabel runs the house and receives the Peronist envoys who arrive from Buenos Aires with plans and quarrels. She is present at every conversation and party to none of them. She is twenty-eight years old.
suggested_refs: The quinta 17 de Octubre, Puerta de Hierro, Madrid, the household's address from 1960

stops.name: Madrid, the marriage at the doctor's house
stops.date_confidence: disputed; 15 November 1961 is the officially announced date, but an alternative account places the ceremony on 2 or 5 January 1961 with the announcement withheld for months. Not resolved here. The coordinates are a Madrid placeholder: the street address of the physician's house is not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: In a Catholic ceremony at the Madrid home of Perón's personal physician, Francisco Flores Tascón, Isabel Martínez becomes the third wife of Juan Perón. He is sixty-six, she is thirty. Eva Perón has been dead nine years and her body is hidden somewhere in Europe by the Argentine military, its location unknown to the man marrying again. There are no photographs of the ceremony in general circulation and the guests are few. Argentina learns of the marriage from an announcement, which is how it learns most things about this household.
suggested_refs: The Madrid residence of Dr. Francisco Flores Tascón, site of the Perón marriage

stops.name: Ezeiza, the first return
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 10 October 1965
stops.campa: She lands at Ezeiza as Juan Perón's personal political delegate, the first of the household to set foot in Argentina since 1955, carrying his signature and his authority to a movement banned from the ballot. She is thirty-four and has never held office of any kind. The crowd at the fence is not there for her; it is there for the absent man whose name she brings. Over the next nine months she will hold more than six hundred meetings across the country, and the Peronist bosses who expect to manage her will find her harder than advertised.
suggested_refs: Ezeiza International Airport, arrival of Perón's personal delegate, 10 October 1965

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the union building on Callao
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1965; the day is not recorded and 20 is a placeholder within the attested month
stops.campa: She takes rooms briefly in Recoleta, then moves into the building of the Luz y Fuerza electrical workers' union on Callao and receives from there. The union hall is neutral ground in a movement at war with itself: Augusto Vandor's wing wants a Peronism without Perón, the loyalists want the man himself back. Isabel sits between them with a letter of authority from Madrid and no faction of her own. She writes to her husband almost daily, in a private hand the public will not read for fifty-two years.
suggested_refs: The Luz y Fuerza union building on Av. Callao, headquarters of the 1965-66 delegate mission

stops.name: Rosario, eight thousand hands in one day
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated 21 November 1965 in the Infobae transcription, correcting a widely repeated October dating
stops.campa: The delegate works the litoral. In Rosario she receives thousands in a single day, standing to shake hands until the little finger swells, and writes it home to Madrid the same night with the callus in the report. The letters from this tour, published by Infobae in 2017, show a woman counting crowds like a professional and reading the movement's men with a cold eye. Nine months of provincial halls and a ledger posted to Spain every night turn a general's wife into a political fact.
stops.quote: En Rosario en un solo día recibí más de 8.000 personas (tengo un callito en el dedo meñique de tantos miles de manos que he estrechado).
stops.quote_source: Isabel Martínez de Perón to Juan Perón, letter of 21 November 1965, in Claudia Peiró, 'En exclusiva: las cartas privadas inéditas de Isabel a Perón, durante una misión en Argentina,' Infobae, 25 June 2017
suggested_refs: The Isabel-to-Perón correspondence of 1965-66, published by Infobae, 25 June 2017

stops.name: Catamarca, emperors and one empress
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated 6 December 1965
stops.campa: In Catamarca, at the far end of the northwest circuit, she writes to Madrid a line that reads one way in 1965 and another after 1974. The tour has taught her what deference looks like from the receiving end: women kneeling to kiss her feet, provincial caudillos taking her measure, a movement running on one absent man's name and one dead woman's photograph. She signs the letters as a wife reporting to a husband. She is also, by this point, the only Peronist authority physically present in Argentina.
stops.quote: Pienso que en la Argentina había muchos emperadores y alguna emperatriz.
stops.quote_source: Isabel Martínez de Perón to Juan Perón, letter of 6 December 1965, in Claudia Peiró, Infobae, 25 June 2017
suggested_refs: The 6 December 1965 letter from Catamarca, in the Infobae correspondence

stops.name: Mendoza, the vote split on purpose
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated 20 April 1966, three days after the Mendoza gubernatorial vote of 17 April
stops.campa: The Mendoza gubernatorial election splits the Peronist vote and denies Vandor's faction the province. Isabel, who has campaigned there against the neoperonistas, reports the result to Madrid as a victory won by losing: the governorship was never the point, the destruction of the rival apparatus was. In the same correspondence Delia Parodi and Vandor are basura and no truce is to be given them. Three years later Vandor is shot dead in his union office by men no court ever convicts of sending.
stops.quote: Hubiera querido brindarte el gobierno de Mendoza pero pienso que es mejor así; lo importante en realidad no era el contubernio sino defenestrar para siempre el cáncer del peronismo.
stops.quote_source: Isabel Martínez de Perón to Juan Perón, letter of 20 April 1966, in Claudia Peiró, Infobae, 25 June 2017
suggested_refs: The 17 April 1966 Mendoza gubernatorial election and the Peronist split

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house of Colonel Alberte
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Spanish record dates the meeting to this stay and hedges it with supuestamente, giving no day. May 1966 is the best available placement and the day is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: At the Buenos Aires house of Lieutenant Colonel Bernardo Alberte, Perón's military delegate, she is introduced to a former police corporal, singer and occultist named José López Rega. The Spanish record hedges the circumstance; the consequence is not in doubt. He attaches himself to her, becomes her secretary, and within eight years will run a ministry, a death squad and the government of Argentina from behind her chair. She is thirty-five. He is what this tour brings home.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires residence of Lt. Col. Bernardo Alberte, reported site of the first López Rega meeting

stops.name: Madrid, the return with the secretary
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 9 July 1966
stops.campa: On the ninth of July, Argentine independence day, she flies back to Madrid with López Rega in the seat beside her. She leaves behind a country reported back to its exiled owner in a wife's handwriting. Eleven days earlier the army has deposed Arturo Illia and installed Onganía, closing the electoral road she has spent the year walking. Puerta de Hierro absorbs the new secretary; he will not leave this household again until Argentina drives him out of the country nine years later.
stops.quote: He aprendido a ver que a los hombres hay que alimentarles sus vanidades.
stops.quote_source: Isabel Martínez de Perón to Juan Perón, letter of 9-10 June 1966, in Claudia Peiró, Infobae, 25 June 2017
suggested_refs: The 9 July 1966 return flight to Madrid, with José López Rega

stops.name: Puerta de Hierro, the coffin from Milan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 3 September 1971
stops.campa: A truck reaches the villa carrying the embalmed body of Eva Perón, hidden in a Milan grave for sixteen years by the Argentine military and handed back by a government trying to buy peace. The coffin is opened in the house. Isabel is set to comb the hair and tend the body of the woman whose place she occupies. Tradition holds that López Rega worked rites over the two women at once, to pass the dead one's power into the living. The corpus carries this pin from Eva's side as well, and from Juan's.
suggested_refs: eva_peron.journey.json, stop 'Madrid, Puerta de Hierro, devuelta a Perón en el exilio'

stops.name: Ezeiza, the second delegation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 7 December 1971
stops.campa: She returns to Argentina a second time as her husband's delegate, and this time the crowd at Ezeiza is partly there for her. The Lanusse dictatorship is negotiating its own exit and Peronism is legal again in everything but name. She is forty and has spent six years learning what the Argentine political class is made of. The men who ran the movement in Perón's absence, the ones she called basura in letters no one has yet read, are obliged to receive her as the household's voice.
suggested_refs: The 7 December 1971 arrival at Ezeiza, second delegate mission

stops.name: Beijing, the mission of a movement
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Spanish record gives 8 to 18 May 1973 for the mission
stops.campa: Between the eighth and the eighteenth of May, days before Cámpora is inaugurated in Buenos Aires as Perón's stand-in, Isabel Martínez de Perón flies to Beijing with López Rega on a mission of the movement rather than of any state. She holds no office and no candidacy; the Perón-Perón ticket does not yet exist and will not be proclaimed until August. She is received as the wife of a man about to retake a country he was thrown out of eighteen years ago, and the reception is a state one.
suggested_refs: The May 1973 Perón delegation to the People's Republic of China

stops.name: Pyongyang, Kim Il-sung receives her
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1973 within the 8-18 May mission; the exact day in Pyongyang is not recorded and 15 is a placeholder
stops.campa: The mission continues to Pyongyang and Kim Il-sung receives her. A dancer from La Rioja, secretary and third wife to an exiled general, shakes hands with the founder of the North Korean state on the strength of a surname she acquired at thirty. Argentina at this moment has a Peronist president who is not Perón, an old man in Madrid packing to come home, and armed factions of its own youth wing preparing to shoot at each other. The delegation flies back to Spain in time for the last act.
suggested_refs: The May 1973 meeting with Kim Il-sung, Pyongyang

stops.name: Morón Air Base, the homecoming diverted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 20 June 1973
stops.campa: Perón comes home for good and something between one and three million people go to Ezeiza to meet him. Snipers of the movement's right open fire on its left from the speakers' platform; the dead are counted in dozens, the wounded in hundreds. The aircraft carrying Perón, Isabel and López Rega is turned away and put down at the Morón air base instead. Eighteen years of exile land on a military runway under army guard, while the crowd assembled to celebrate the return is busy killing its own.
suggested_refs: Base Aérea Militar Morón, landing site of Perón's return flight, 20 June 1973

stops.name: Teatro Colón, the ticket proclaimed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 5 August 1973
stops.campa: At the Teatro Colón the Justicialist movement proclaims the Perón-Perón ticket: the general for president, his wife for vice president, over the objection of half his lieutenants and of every faction that expected second place for itself. López Rega has pushed for her hardest. On the twenty-third of September the ticket takes 61.85 percent of the vote, the largest mandate in Argentine electoral history. She has been a candidate for seven weeks and a figure in politics for eight years.
suggested_refs: The 5 August 1973 proclamation ceremony at the Teatro Colón

stops.name: Casa Rosada, sworn in as vice president
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 12 October 1973
stops.campa: On the twelfth of October Juan Perón takes the presidential sash for the third time, twenty-eight years after the seventeenth of October that made him, and Isabel Martínez de Perón is sworn in beside him as vice president of the Republic, the first woman to hold that office. The old man is seventy-seven and visibly ill. The Montoneros who fought for his return are being expelled from the movement in public. López Rega holds the Ministry of Social Welfare and its budget. The arithmetic of the succession is in every newspaper.
suggested_refs: juan_peron.journey.json, stop 'Perón and Isabel take office, October 1973'

stops.name: Quinta de Olivos, the death of Perón
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 1 July 1974; she had been sworn in as acting president on 29 June, the day after the heart attacks of 28 June
stops.campa: Juan Perón dies at the Olivos residence in the early afternoon, three days after the heart attacks that put the government in his wife's hands. Isabel goes on television that evening and announces the death of the man and her own constitutional assumption of the presidency in a single broadcast; her voice breaks in the middle of it. She is forty-three years old and the first woman anywhere to hold the title of President of a republic. The corpus carries this ground from Perón's side as the place he dies.
stops.quote: Con gran dolor debo transmitir al pueblo el fallecimiento de un verdadero apóstol de la paz y la no violencia; asumo constitucionalmente la primera magistratura del país.
stops.quote_source: Isabel Perón, televised address on the death of Juan Perón, 1 July 1974, recording 'Isabel anuncia la muerte de Perón'
suggested_refs: juan_peron.journey.json, stop 'Death at Olivos, 1 July 1974'

stops.name: Casa Rosada, the anti-terrorism law and the state of siege
stops.date_confidence: attested; the anti-terrorism law is dated 30 September 1974 and the state of siege 6 November 1974. The stop is pinned to the first
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of September she signs an anti-terrorism law widening what the state may do to its enemies; on the sixth of November she declares a state of siege and suspends constitutional guarantees, habeas corpus among them. Argentina will remain under state of siege for nine years. The instruments the junta of 1976 will use against her own party are drafted and signed by a Peronist president in her fourth month, against organizations that were, eighteen months earlier, inside the movement that elected her.
suggested_refs: Ley 20.840 of 30 September 1974 and the state of siege decree of 6 November 1974

stops.name: Quinta de Olivos, Eva laid beside him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 17 November 1974
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November the body of Eva Perón, brought home from Madrid on the president's order, is laid at Olivos beside the coffin of Juan Perón in a chapel built for the purpose. The three of them are in one house: the founder, the saint, and the third wife who combed the saint's hair in a Madrid villa and now governs the country the other two made. Six months earlier Perón died in this building. The corpus carries this ground from Eva's side and from his.
suggested_refs: eva_peron.journey.json, stop 'Olivos, de vuelta en la patria, 1974'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Triple A count
stops.date_confidence: attested as a running total: nearly 300 murders between late 1973 and late 1974, some 600 in the group's whole existence. The stop is pinned to the end of 1974 with the day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: By late 1974 the Argentine Anticommunist Alliance has murdered close to three hundred people in about fifteen months, and will reach some six hundred before it stops. It works out of López Rega's Ministry of Social Welfare, with police cars and state petrol. On the thirtieth of September, in this same city, Chilean agents of Pinochet's DINA blow up General Carlos Prats and his wife in their car; the atlas carries that killing from the Chilean side. The president signs what her secretary puts in front of her.
suggested_refs: augusto_pinochet.journey.json, stop on the Prats assassination, Buenos Aires 1974

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, Operativo Independencia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 5 February 1975
stops.campa: By decree she orders the armed forces into Tucumán to annihilate the ERP guerrilla foco in the sugar hills. Operativo Independencia hands the army a legal war, a free province and its first clandestine detention centre, the Escuelita de Famaillá. The methods rehearsed here through 1975 become the methods of the whole country after March 1976. The order carries the signature of the constitutional president of Argentina, thirteen months before the same army takes her off a helicopter at gunpoint.
suggested_refs: Decree 261/75 of 5 February 1975 and the Escuelita de Famaillá, Tucumán

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Rodrigazo and the first strike
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1975 for the Rodrigazo measures and July 1975 for the general strike; the day of the June measures is not fixed here and defaults to 01
stops.campa: Economy Minister Celestino Rodrigo doubles utility rates and transport fares and devalues the peso by more than half; consumer prices double between May and August. The Rodrigazo destroys what is left of the government's hold on labour. In July the CGT calls a two-day general strike, the first ever called against a Peronist administration, and Argentina discovers that the movement's own labour federation is in the street against a president named Perón. Inflation was running near twelve percent a year when she took office.
suggested_refs: The Rodrigazo of June 1975 and the CGT general strike of July 1975

stops.name: Madrid, López Rega goes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 19 July 1975
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of July, with the unions in the street demanding his head, José López Rega leaves Argentina for Spain, handed the courtesy title of ambassador extraordinary on his way out the door. He has run the Ministry of Social Welfare, the death squad, the presidential astrology and the president's daily calendar since 1973. Isabel loses the man who made her and keeps everything he built. She takes medical leave in September and comes back in October to a government nobody obeys.
suggested_refs: The July 1975 flight of José López Rega to Spain

stops.name: Casa Rosada, the decree of annihilation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 6 October 1975
stops.campa: On the sixth of October she signs decrees extending to the whole national territory what Tucumán has been rehearsing: the armed forces are to annihilate the action of subversive elements everywhere in Argentina. The generals now hold a written order from a civilian president to do what they will do to thirty thousand people. Five months later the same officers depose her. The documents are read out at their trials in 1985 and cited again in the Mendoza case brought against her thirty-one years later.
suggested_refs: Decrees 2770, 2771 and 2772 of 6 October 1975

stops.name: Aeroparque Jorge Newbery, the arrest on the tarmac
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the sources place the landing at roughly ten past three in the morning of 24 March 1976
stops.campa: She works past midnight at the Casa Rosada trying to head off a business lockout, then boards the presidential helicopter for Olivos. It sets down at Aeroparque instead, on a pretext of mechanical trouble. General José Rogelio Villarreal is waiting on the tarmac. She tries to negotiate: Congress kept open, military ministers in her cabinet, and is told that a country has been drawn for her which does not exist. It is a little after three in the morning and no one in Argentina comes into the street for her.
stops.quote: Señora, las Fuerzas Armadas han decidido tomar el control político del país y usted queda arrestada.
stops.quote_source: Gen. José Rogelio Villarreal to Isabel Perón, Aeroparque, 24 March 1976, as printed in TN, '24 de marzo: del horror a la esperanza'. Infobae's 2019 reconstruction gives the same exchange in different words: 'usted ha sido destituida'
suggested_refs: Aeroparque Jorge Newbery, landing site of the presidential helicopter, 24 March 1976
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Golpe de Estado en Argentina de 1976'
TN, '24 de marzo: del horror a la esperanza'
Infobae, 'La historia secreta de cómo se gestó el golpe del 24 de marzo de 1976', 24 March 2019

stops.name: El Messidor, Villa La Angostura, the lake for a wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to late March 1976 for the transfer; about seven months here, then further custody. The exact day of arrival is not recorded and 25 is a placeholder
stops.campa: She is flown south to Neuquén and shut up in El Messidor, the provincial governor's residence on the shore of Nahuel Huapi, with her housekeeper Rosarito for company and the lake for a wall. Seven months here, then transfers including the naval arsenal at Azul; five years of house arrest in all, the full sequence of addresses never published. The junta charges her with corruption and never with the decrees. Outside, the machinery those decrees authorized is running at full speed.
suggested_refs: El Messidor, Villa La Angostura, Neuquén, first detention site of the deposed president

stops.name: Recoleta Cemetery, Eva goes into the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 22 October 1976
stops.campa: The body of Eva Perón, which Isabel brought home to Olivos in 1974, is buried in the Duarte vault at Recoleta by the admirals who imprisoned her, some of whom have discussed dropping it into the sea instead. The cemetery already holds Julio Argentino Roca, sixty-two years in the ground, and Aimé Tschiffely, twenty-two. The woman who returned Eva to Argentina is under guard on a Patagonian lake and is not consulted. The corpus now carries this vault from three sides.
suggested_refs: eva_peron.journey.json, stop dated 1976-10-22; julio_argentino_roca.journey.json and tschiffely.journey.json, Recoleta stops

stops.name: Madrid-Barajas, flown into exile
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1981; the day is not recorded and defaults to 01
stops.campa: Released after five years of house arrest, she is flown out of Argentina to Madrid. The junta that deposed her is five years into the Process and a year from the Malvinas. In the Buenos Aires she leaves behind, Victoria Ocampo has died two years ago and Jorge Luis Borges is writing through these years without naming what is happening in them; the corpus tracks both across the same city and the same decade. Isabel Perón lands at Barajas at fifty, with no party, no country to return to and a file that will follow her.

stops.name: Puerta de Hierro, the same address again
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1981 for the resettlement and February 1985 for the party resignation; the month and day of the return to Puerta de Hierro are not recorded
stops.campa: She settles again at Puerta de Hierro, in the Madrid geography the household has occupied since 1960, and keeps the titular leadership of the Justicialist Party at a distance until February 1985, when she resigns it. Peronism reorganizes in Argentina without her and never asks her back. She stops giving interviews. From this point the record of her life is made almost entirely of things other people do about her: trials, tributes, plaques, busts, invitations she declines.
suggested_refs: Her February 1985 resignation as titular head of the Partido Justicialista

stops.name: Congreso de la Nación, guest of honour at the restoration
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1983; the sources give the month, and 10 December is the inauguration date of Raúl Alfonsín
stops.campa: Raúl Alfonsín takes the presidential sash at the Congreso and Isabel Perón is a guest of honour: the constitutional president the army removed, present at the restoration of the order it broke. She comes back in May 1984 for political talks and in 1988 over probate on Juan Perón's estate, and after that she stops coming. Argentina is opening the trials of the juntas. Her own decrees of October 1975 are going into the evidence, and the signature on them is hers.

stops.name: Barajas, the bomb that was found
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year 1984 is all the single source gives, and month and day default to 01-01. The whole episode rests on one Peronist outlet reached through a web archive
stops.campa: A bomb is placed aboard an Aerolíneas Argentinas flight carrying her; Argentine airport security finds it before it goes off and the aircraft lands at Barajas intact. She is reported to have said on the tarmac that nobody dies five minutes ahead of God's plan. President Alfonsín condemns the attempt from Buenos Aires. The episode is carried in one Peronist outlet reached only through a web archive, and stands here as thinly sourced rather than established; the quote in particular has no second witness.

stops.quote_source: Attributed to Isabel Perón at Barajas, 1984, in es.wikipedia.org, 'María Estela Martínez de Perón', section 'Atentados contra su vida', citing agendaperonista.com.ar via the Wayback Machine

stops.name: Villafranca del Castillo, the townhouse with a gate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2001 for the sale of Puerta de Hierro and the move; no month or day recorded, defaulted to 01-01. Spanish citizenship obtained in 2000
stops.campa: She sells the Puerta de Hierro estate that housed Perón's exile and moves to a townhouse in Villafranca del Castillo, an urbanización west of Madrid inside the municipality of Villanueva de la Cañada. Spanish citizenship since 2000, a pension, a small circle, no calls to Buenos Aires. The last living link to the atlas's Madrid Peronist geography is now a suburban house behind a gate, thirty kilometres from the villa where the coffin was opened and the hair was combed in 1971.

stops.name: Villafranca del Castillo, the arrest and the refused extradition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 12 January 2007; the Audiencia Nacional refusal is dated 28 March 2008 and the Argentine Supreme Court dismissal 21 June 2017
stops.campa: A judge in Mendoza orders her arrest over forced disappearances committed under her government, and Spanish police detain her at the house. On the twenty-eighth of March 2008 the Audiencia Nacional refuses the extradition: the limitation period has run, and the court declines to classify the charges as crimes against humanity. In 2017 Argentina's Supreme Court dismisses the petitions seeking to compel her interrogation. She is seventy-six at the arrest and will not be tried anywhere, for anything.
suggested_refs: The Audiencia Nacional ruling of 28 March 2008 refusing Argentina's extradition request

stops.name: Senado de la Nación, the bust on the Day of Loyalty
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the Senate ceremony. Other reporting places Vice President Villarruel at Isabel Perón's Madrid house on the same 17 October 2024; both datings are carried here and the conflict is not resolved
stops.campa: On the Día de la Lealtad, Vice President Victoria Villarruel unveils a bust of Isabel Perón inside the Argentine Senate, naming her the first woman to hold the vice presidency and the presidency and blaming those who left her at the mercy of terrorism. Other reporting puts Villarruel at the Madrid house on the same day. Peronism disowned her, the Spanish courts declined to hand her over, the Argentine courts declined to try her, and a government of the new right has made her a monument in the chamber she once presided over.

stops.name: Villafranca del Castillo, no grave to end at
stops.date_confidence: the subject is living; this stop is dated to the last well-attested contact with her, and is open at the near end. The March 2024 photograph and the Villarruel visit both fall in this year
stops.campa: In March 2024, at ninety-three, she is photographed at home receiving a prize from a Spanish cultural association, the first published picture of her in decades. Pope Francis sends a video greeting in October saying he remembers her and prays for her. She is alive, in Madrid, and there is no tomb, so this journey has no last stone to stand on. Juan Perón is in San Vicente, Eva Perón is under Recoleta, and the third of that household is behind a gate in a suburb, uninterred and unjudged.
